prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Sign Language Translation (SLT) is fundamentally challenged by the visual-spatial nature of the language, which relies heavily on context that is often absent in standard sentence-level modeling. In isolation, sign language video is rife with ambiguity due to homonyms (different meanings sharing similar manual movements) and the use of spatial indexing (pointing to objects or referencing previously established topics). Current state-of-the-art systems typically process signing sequences as isolated events, ignoring the broader discourse and the physical environment. Furthermore, existing supervision is often weak and noisy, relying on subtitles that are temporally misaligned with the signing. We need a system that moves beyond isolated video-to-text translation and incorporates the extrinsic cues that human interpreters instinctively use to resolve ambiguity.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that SLT performance can be significantly improved by mimicking the cognitive process of a human interpreter, who relies on "contextual cues" to disambiguate signing. We posit that a pre-trained Large Language Model (LLM) can act as a reasoning engine to synthesize heterogeneous information sources. Specifically, we believe that by supplementing the raw signing video with **environmental context** (descriptions of the visual background) and **discourse context** (previous translations), we can resolve ambiguities related to homonyms and co-references that are otherwise unsolvable.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose a multi-modal translation framework that leverages a pre-trained LLM to generate spoken language from a composite input sequence. The methodology focuses on converting various contextual signals into a unified textual representation compatible with the LLM.

1.  **Visual Sign Encoding:** We will extract dense spatiotemporal features from the signing video using a video encoder. To bridge the modality gap, we will train a lightweight mapping network (a projection layer) to transform these visual embeddings into the input token space of the LLM.
2.  **Pseudo-Gloss Integration:** We will utilize an Isolated Sign Language Recognition (ISLR) model to generate "pseudo-glosses"—a noisy, intermediate sequence of sign labels. These will serve as a textual anchor to guide the LLM's attention.
3.  **Environmental Context Extraction:** To capture the scene context (crucial when signers point to objects on a screen or in the background), we will employ an off-the-shelf image captioning model. We will crop the signer out of the frame and generate textual descriptions of the background, extracting keywords to provide semantic cues about the environment.
4.  **Discourse Context (Auto-Regression):** We will incorporate the translation of the *previous* sentence as an input. During inference, this will be the model's own previous prediction, allowing the LLM to maintain tense consistency and track semantic topics across sentence boundaries.
5.  **LLM Fine-Tuning:** All inputs (projected visual features, pseudo-glosses, background descriptions, and previous sentences) will be serialized into a single prompt sequence with specific separators. We will fine-tune the LLM (using parameter-efficient methods like LoRA) to generate the final spoken language translation based on this rich context.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Context-Aware Framework:** We aim to establish a new paradigm for SLT that treats translation as a context-dependent task rather than an isolated video processing problem.
2.  **Integration of Environmental Cues:** We expect to demonstrate that background visual information—often treated as noise—is actually a critical semantic signal for interpreted footage.
3.  **LLM-Driven Synthesis:** We will provide a theoretical proof-of-concept for using LLMs to fuse noisy visual representations with high-level textual context to resolve linguistic ambiguities like homonymy and spatial referencing.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We designed and executed a framework for Open-Vocabulary Sign Language Translation (SLT) that integrated visual features with contextual textual cues (pseudo-glosses, background descriptions, and previous sentence translations) using a fine-tuned Large Language Model (LLM).

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **BOBSL (British Sign Language):**
        *   Source: ~1,400 hours of interpreted TV broadcasts.
        *   Training Split: 689k video-sentence pairs (filtered to 1-20 seconds duration). Vocabulary: 86k words.
        *   Validation Split (SENT-VAL): 1,973 aligned sentences. Vocabulary: 3,528 words.
        *   Test Split (SENT-TEST): 20,870 aligned sentences. Vocabulary: 13,641 words.
    *   **How2Sign (American Sign Language):**
        *   Source: 80 hours of instructional videos (10 topics).
        *   Training Split: 31,128 sentences. Vocabulary: 15.7k words.
        *   Validation Split: 1,741 sentences. Vocabulary: 3.2k words.
        *   Test Split: 2,322 sentences. Vocabulary: 3.7k words.

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **BLEU-4 (B4):** Geometric mean of 4-gram precision with brevity penalty.
    *   **BLEURT (B-RT):** Learned metric capturing semantic similarities.
    *   **ROUGE-L (R-L):** Longest common subsequence measure.
    *   **CIDEr:** Consensus-based captioning metric using TF-IDF.
    *   **Intersection over Union (IoU):** Computed on lemmatized token sets; synonyms not penalized.
    *   **LLM Score:** A novel metric using GPT-4o-mini to score translations from 0 (worst) to 5 (best) based on detailed reasoning, focusing on key nouns/verbs over pronouns.

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **Video-Only Baselines:** Albanie, Sincan, GFSLT, Sign2GPT (with and without Prototype-Guided Pre-training/PGP).
    *   **Oracle Baselines:** Sincan variants using ground truth previous sentences and ground truth-derived spottings.
    *   **How2Sign Baselines:** SSLT, SSVP-SLT, Fla-LLM, VAP.

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Visual Encoder:** Video-Swin (pre-trained for ISLR). 16-frame inputs with sliding window (stride 2). Output: 768-dimensional embeddings.
    *   **Mapping Network:** 2-layer MLP with GELU activation (projecting 768 dim to 4096 dim). Randomly initialized.
    *   **LLM:** Llama 3 (8B parameters). Pre-trained text embeddings were frozen.
    *   **Fine-tuning:** Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) on query and value projectors. Configuration: Rank 4, Alpha 16, Dropout 0.05.
    *   **Context Extraction:**
        *   *Background:* BLIP2 image captioning applied to frames sampled at 1 fps (signer cropped out).
        *   *Pseudo-glosses:* Extracted via ISLR classifier on Video-Swin features.
    *   **Training Parameters:**
        *   Hardware: 4 H100 GPUs.
        *   Batch Size: 2 per GPU (Accumulated).
        *   Optimizer: Adam (Learning rate 0.0001).
        *   Precision: bfloat16 with FlashAttention-2.
        *   Epochs: 10 (BOBSL), 15 (How2Sign). Warmup: 5 epochs. Gradient clipping: 1.0.
    *   **Augmentations:**
        *   Word dropping (0-50% in textual cues).
        *   Cue dropping (50% probability per cue).
        *   Previous Sentence: Random sampling (50/50) between Ground Truth (GT) and Predicted previous sentences during training.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

*   **Impact of Background Description:** We observed that background descriptions successfully disambiguated homonyms and reference pointing. In one instance, a signer pointed to a screen where a rhino horn was visible; the pseudo-gloss incorrectly identified "elephant," but the background cue allowed the model to correctly predict "rhino horn."
*   **Resolution of Ambiguity:** We found that background cues helped resolve pronoun ambiguity. For a sign sequence that could mean "He's looking" or "She's looking," the presence of a woman in the background description steered the model to correctly predict "She."
*   **Contextual Complementarity:** We noted that cues were complementary. In a sample where the ground truth was "Beautiful petals that wave about in the wind," the background cue provided "flower" and the previous sentence cue provided "wind." The model combined these to predict "They're beautiful flowers and they're wafting in the wind."
*   **Information Recovery:** We observed cases where the signer did not sign a specific subject (e.g., "jellyfish"), but the background description contained the specific animal name, allowing the model to generate a precise translation rather than a generic one (e.g., "biggest animals" vs "largest jellyfish").
*   **Conflicting Cues:** We identified limitations where background information hindered translation. In one case involving a rock formation, the background context overwhelmed the visual signing cues, leading to an incorrect translation.
*   **Grammatical Challenges:** Despite improvements, we observed the model occasionally struggled with distinguishing between questions and statements, and frequently missed negations.
*   **Comparison to Baselines:** Even without extra cues, our video-only model significantly outperformed previous state-of-the-art methods (Sign2GPT and GFSLT) on the BOBSL dataset across all metrics.
*   **Augmentation Effects:** We observed that applying augmentations (dropping words and cues) reduced model sensitivity to noise and reliance on specific modalities, leading to higher validation scores. Incorporating predicted previous sentences during training reduced the domain gap at inference time.

In this example, the ground truth (GT) translation has common words or semantics with the background context (e.g., flower), and the previous sentence (e.g., wind).

  - Filename: figure_2.png
  - Caption: Figure 2. Method overview: The input prompt combines contextual cues, the background descriptions and previous sentences, with the information from the current video sequence, specifically visual features and pseudo-glosses. Visual features corresponding to the signer {V } are extracted using a pre-trained Video-Swin model, which are projected to text space with a learnable mapping network. We obtain pseudo-glosses {P} by passing the Video-Swin features through the pre-trained ISLR Classifier (*Video-Swin here denotes the layers except the last one of the ISLR model). The background captions, obtained from an off-the-shelf image captioner, are summarised into a list of keywords, which we refer to as background descriptions. During training, we randomly sample previous GT sentences and previous predictions, while during inference, the model uses its previous prediction in an auto-regressive manner. In practice, we include prompts that instruct the model on sign language translation and describe each input. We supervise the predicted translation output by comparing it against the ground truth, e.g., ‘As pagans, the Romans worshipped many gods and spirits’ in this example. Note that we do not use ground-truth glosses – they are displayed on the bottom right (e.g. roman, many...) only for illustration.
--------------------------------------------------

  - Filename: figure_3.png
  - Caption: Figure 3. Qualitative analysis: We present visual examples to show how different cues affect the translation results. Starting with visual features, we incrementally add pseudo-glosses (PG), the predicted previous sentence (Prev), and the background description (BG). We observe that the previous sentence helps translation performance by providing further context (top left, bottom right). The background description also helps for pronoun referencing (top right), place names (middle left), pointing gestures (middle right), and object referencing (bottom left). However, the background can also in some cases hinder translation (bottom right). We refer to Sec. 4.5 for detailed comments.
--------------------------------------------------

prompt.text:
Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
\end{quotation}
```

## Illustrations, graphs, and photographs
All graphics should be centered.
In \LaTeX, avoid using the \texttt{center} environment for this purpose, as this adds potentially unwanted whitespace.
Instead use
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \centering
\end{verbatim}}
```
at the beginning of your figure.

Please ensure that any point you wish to make is resolvable in a printed copy of the paper. Resize fonts in figures to match the font in the body text, and choose line widths that render effectively in print.

When placing figures in \LaTeX, it's almost always best to use \verb+\includegraphics+, and to specify the figure width as a multiple of the line width as in the example below

```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
   \usepackage{graphicx} ...
   \includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]
                   {myfile.pdf}
\end{verbatim}}
```

references.text:
## Problem Statement
Current approaches to Sign Language Translation (SLT) predominantly operate in an isolated manner, treating individual sentence-level video clips as independent translation tasks. However, sign languages are inherently visual-spatial and heavily dependent on contextual discourse. Key grammatical elements—such as spatial indexing (referencing previously established entities), topic-comment structures (where tense or subject is set once and implied thereafter), and homonyms (signs with identical movements but context-dependent meanings)—render sentence-level translation ill-defined when stripped of context.

Furthermore, the field faces a scarcity of large-scale, high-quality parallel corpora. We must rely on datasets like BOBSL, which contain broadcast footage with subtitles. These subtitles provide weak and noisy supervision; they are temporally aligned to speech rather than signing, and often involve simplification or omission inherent to interpretation. Existing architectures fail to effectively leverage the broader multimodal context (visual background, previous discourse) necessary to disambiguate these signals and resolve the noise in open-vocabulary settings.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that SLT performance can be significantly enhanced by mimicking the cognitive process of human interpreters, who rely on multiple contextual cues rather than visual signing alone. We propose a framework that treats SLT as a conditional text generation task governed by a pre-trained Large Language Model (LLM).

Specifically, we posit that by integrating **four distinct information streams**—(1) continuous visual signing features, (2) automatic pseudo-gloss transcriptions, (3) background visual scene descriptions, and (4) previous sentence translations—we can ground the translation in its proper semantic context. We believe that fine-tuning a foundational LLM (Llama3) with these inputs will allow the model to suppress noise in automatic glossing and resolve linguistic ambiguities (such as reference resolution and homonyms) that are unsolvable from the signing video alone.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will develop a multimodal translation framework that projects visual and textual cues into a shared embedding space to prompt a pre-trained LLM. The methodology comprises input extraction, feature projection, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning.

### 1. Input Modalities and Feature Extraction

We define the input space as a tuple of four modalities: $\{V, P, B, S_{prev}\}$.

**A. Visual Features ($V$):**
We will utilize a Video-Swin Transformer backbone, pre-trained on the BOBSL dataset for Isolated Sign Language Recognition (ISLR).
*   **Input Processing:** We ingest the video as a sequence of frames. To capture fine-grained temporal details, we apply a sliding window of 16 frames with a stride $s$ (e.g., $s=2$).
*   **Formulation:** Let $f(\cdot)$ be the video encoder (excluding the final classification layer). The visual features sequence $V_{1:F}$ is defined as:
    $$ V_{1:F} = \{ v_i \in \mathbb{R}^{768} \mid i = 1, \dots, F \} $$
    where $v_i$ is the spatio-temporal average of the penultimate layer output for the $i$-th window, and $F$ is the total number of features per sentence.

**B. Pseudo-Glosses ($P$):**
We will generate an intermediate textual representation using the same ISLR Video-Swin model (denoted as classifier $C(\cdot)$).
*   **Extraction:** We apply $C$ in a sliding window to obtain a sequence of sign category predictions.
*   **Formulation:** The pseudo-gloss sequence $P_{1:G}$ is defined as:
    $$ P_{1:G} = \{ p_j \in \mathcal{V}_{ISLR} \mid j = 1, \dots, G \} $$
    where $\mathcal{V}_{ISLR}$ is the classifier vocabulary (approx. 8,697 signs).
*   **Noise Handling:** We will perform simple repetition grouping but will **not** threshold by confidence. We purposely retain noisy, over-generated glosses to allow the LLM to learn relevance and filtering implicitly.

**C. Background Description ($B$):**
To capture the visual context (e.g., an image on a screen behind the signer that explains a pointed reference), we will employ an image captioning model (BLIP2).
*   **Processing:** We will crop the signer from the frame to isolate the background. We sample frames at 1 fps.
*   **Text Generation:** We generate captions for sampled frames, aggregate them, and filter for unique words, removing standard stopwords. This results in a bag-of-keywords set $B$.

**D. Previous Sentence ($S_{prev}$):**
We incorporate the textual translation of the immediately preceding sentence to provide discourse context.
*   **Training:** We will alternate between the ground truth previous sentence ($S_{prev}^{GT}$) and a pre-computed predicted previous sentence ($S_{prev}^{Pred}$).
*   **Inference:** The model will operate auto-regressively, using its own output from step $t-1$ as input for step $t$.

### 2. Architecture and Projection

**Visual-to-Text Mapping:**
Since $V$ exists in $\mathbb{R}^{768}$ and the LLM expects token embeddings in $\mathbb{R}^{4096}$ (for Llama3-8B), we will introduce a learnable mapping network $\mathcal{M}$.
*   **Structure:** $\mathcal{M}$ will be a 2-layer Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) with a GELU activation function.
*   **Operation:** $\hat{V} = \mathcal{M}(V)$, where $\hat{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{F \times 4096}$.

**LLM Backbone:**
We will utilize **Llama3-8B** as the core decoder.
*   **Input Sequence Construction:** We will concatenate the inputs into a single sequence with specific prompts serving as separators. The prompt structure will be:
    `[Instruction] [Prompt_V] M(V) [Prompt_P] P [Prompt_B] B [Prompt_S] S_{prev}`
*   **Instruction:** "You are an AI assistant designed to interpret a video of a sign language signing sequence and translate it into English."

### 3. Training Strategy and Fine-Tuning

We will freeze the pre-trained weights of the Llama3 backbone and the text embedding layer to preserve language generation capabilities. We will train **only** the mapping network $\mathcal{M}$ and specific LLM adapters.

**Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA):**
We will apply LoRA to the attention layers of the LLM.
*   **Targets:** Query ($W_q$) and Value ($W_v$) projection matrices.
*   **Hyperparameters:** Rank $r=4$, Scaling factor $\alpha=16$, Dropout $= 0.05$.

**Objective Function:**
We utilize standard Cross-Entropy Loss over the target vocabulary $\mathcal{V}_{LLM}$ ($128k$ tokens).
$$ \mathcal{L} = - \sum_{t=1}^{T} \log P(y_t \mid y_{<t}, \text{Context}) $$
where $y$ represents the tokens of the target spoken sentence.

**Robustness Augmentations:**
To prevent over-reliance on any single modality and simulate inference noise, we will implement the following during training:
1.  **Word Dropping:** Randomly omit $0\%$ to $50\%$ of words within textual cues ($P, B, S_{prev}$).
2.  **Cue Dropping:** Randomly omit entire cues with $50\%$ probability.
3.  **Context Switching:** Randomly sample between $S_{prev}^{GT}$ and $S_{prev}^{Pred}$ with $50\%$ probability to bridge the train-test domain gap.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Context-Aware Architecture:** We expect to define the first SLT framework that successfully integrates background visual cues (via captioning) and discourse history (via previous predictions) to resolve high-context linguistic ambiguities.
2.  **Noise Resilience:** By feeding unfiltered pseudo-glosses and background keywords to an LLM, we aim to demonstrate that large-scale language models can effectively act as denoising filters for weak upstream signals in sign language processing.
3.  **Protocol Definition:** We will establish a rigorous methodology for using auto-regressive decoding in continuous SLT, specifically addressing the error propagation inherent in using predicted previous sentences as context.

preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

agent.name: none
agent.how: no coding agent: a 23-stage prompt-chain pipeline over the Anthropic Messages API

network.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).

tools.permissions: no tool calls (requests carry model, messages, max_tokens); generated experiments run as plain subprocesses in the container

preinstalled.zh: python:3.11 bookworm；上游代码按 PYTHONPATH 使用；pdflatex + bibtex；CPU 版 PyTorch 和 numpy、scipy、scikit-learn、pandas、matplotlib 等（constraints.txt 固定）
preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

agent.name: none
agent.how: no external coding agent: EvoScientist's in-process sub-agents (LangChain deepagents)

tools.permissions: think_tool, deepagents built-ins, EvoSkills skills and an execute shell; skill_manager not registered; no search tool

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
